     D. Contract changes

     D.1 Registry identity/provenance — two APIs with genuinely different 
     guarantees, not one loader
     with a boolean flag. Rev 4's load_registry() returning a usable
     VerifiedRegistry plus a
     "approval_pending": true flag conflated "content-verified" with "approved"
     — a candidate that
     merely passed recomputation could still be consumed by production code,
     defeating the point of an
     approval gate. Split into two named functions with different contracts:
     1. load_candidate_registry_for_phase9_audit() — usable now, before
        approval. Runs
        recomputation (recomputes the entire registry from the three frozen
        input files via the
        unmodified selection pipeline and compares it field-for-field to the
        committed JSON, including
        frozen_date now that it's confirmed to be a hardcoded constant with
        nothing legitimate to
        exclude) plus schema/internal-consistency checks. No approval anchor
        required or checked. This is
        what --check, fault tests, and synthetic validation use.
     2. load_registry() — the production/Phase-10+ entry point. Requires a
        separate, external approval
        record (below) to exist and match; raises Phase9NotApproved if the 
        anchor is absent —
        it does not return a partially-usable object with a pending flag. If the
        anchor exists but
        doesn't match the current registry's recomputed hash, it raises a
        distinct tamper error. This
        makes "Phase 10 cannot start before Phase 9 approval" a mechanical
        property of the loader Phase
        10+ code would naturally reach for, not a documentation convention
        someone could bypass by
        calling the wrong function.
     3. External approval anchor: a new, separate record —
        datasets_v3/PHASE9_APPROVAL.json — holding
        {approved_registry_sha256, approved_commit, approved_date}, written by a
        distinct code path the
        normal freeze/regeneration script never calls. approved_commit is the
        SHA of the correction
        commit that introduces the exact registry content being approved — not a
        later status-
        advancement commit — so the lineage reads candidate commit → approval
        record → (separately) the
        commit that advances LAST_COMPLETED_PHASE in CLAUDE.md. This correction 
        builds the mechanism
        and both functions; it does not populate the anchor, because Phase 9
        isn't approved yet.
        Populating it becomes the literal first, separate, auditable action once
        you approve — a few
        lines, one commit, distinct from all the code fixes here. A file inside
        the same writable repo is
        not an external security boundary by itself, so this is described
        precisely as a separately
        reviewed approval record anchored to the reviewed commit, not a
        cryptographic guarantee.
     4. Bypass closure:
        scan_strings/scan_operations/scan_compositions/held_out_values stop
        accepting a bare dict via reg=. They accept only a
        VerifiedCandidateRegistry instance (the
        thin wrapper function 1 returns). Fault tests get a distinct,
        separately-named test-only
        constructor (_unverified_registry_for_tests()) that production code
        never imports — stated
        plainly that Python can't hard-enforce this, only naming convention plus
        a fault test asserting no
        production import path reaches the raw loader.
     5. Deep immutability, not just a frozen wrapper: @dataclass(frozen=True)
        only blocks reassigning
        the top-level attribute, not mutating a nested dict/list inside it. Fix:
        the wrapper stores the
        canonical registry as serialized JSON text; every accessor
        (.section(name), etc.) returns
        json.loads() of that stored text — a fresh deep copy on every read, so a
        caller mutating a
        returned object can never corrupt the stored original. Regression test:
        call an accessor, mutate
        the returned object in place, call the accessor again, assert the second
        result is unaffected.

     D.2 Allowed operations per field — 4 layers, and the subtraction now 
     provably works, because
     there's only one vocabulary, not two. Rev 3/4's flaw: the semantic layer
     said employment → {filter, ranking} while the held-out-families constant is
     {argmax_topk, group_by, limit_only} —
     "ranking" != "argmax_topk", so a literal set-subtraction semantic - 
     held_out would never actually
     remove ranking, silently leaving it training-eligible (the opposite of
     intended, and worse than
     before). Fix: stop inventing softer synonyms for the semantic layer — reuse
     the exact frozen
     construct names everywhere, so eligibility subtraction is a plain,
     provably-correct set difference
     on identical strings, not a translation the code could get wrong:
     1. field_semantic_operations — what's meaningful for a field, including
        held-out operations
        where they make sense, named with the same literal strings as
        HELD_OUT_OPERATIONS
        (holdout_v3.py's existing frozen constant) wherever applicable:
        employment →
        {filter, argmax_topk} (not "ranking"); child-table fields
        (certifications/processes/
        services) and categorical company fields → {filter, aggregation, 
        group_by}.
        aggregation here means ungrouped scalar aggregation only (COUNT/SUM with
        no GROUP BY)
        — a sibling of group_by, never a parent/hierarchy containing it,
        resolving the ambiguity
        directly: the three already-frozen held-out names (argmax_topk,
        group_by, limit_only) are
        never subtypes of anything else in this taxonomy, they're leaves.
     2. query_level_constructs — argmax_topk, group_by, limit_only, tagged as
        structural/
        query-shape operations that pair with an eligible field from layer 1
        (limit_only is
        field-agnostic — arbitrary row sampling, doesn't require a field pairing
        at all, so it's excluded
        globally regardless of any per-field policy — see the fault test in E
        for this specific case).
     3. field_specific_restrictions — sourced verbatim from README, not
        invented: Primary OEMs
        excluded from group_by/argmax_topk (composite-string reason,
        README:537-538); Address gets
        no aggregation of any kind (README:538); row_id — join always allowed,
        filter allowed
        only when the question explicitly names a record (README:541-543);
        company — filtering
        unrestricted.
     4. field_training_eligible_operations (derived) =
        field_semantic_operations[f] - HELD_OUT_OPERATIONS (literal set
        difference on the shared vocabulary, machine-tested by asserting
        this equation for every field), further constrained by layer 3's named
        restrictions. Evaluation/
        probe generation (Phase 22) consumes layers 1+3 directly, unfiltered by
        the subtraction, since the
        operation-heldout probe specifically needs those constructs to exist in
        dev/test.
     5. This per-field map is a candidate-generation-time heuristic, never the 
        authoritative
        eligibility gate. The real, existing gate — already frozen, fixed in D.4
        — is running the actual
        SQL-construct scanner (operation_families_present) against a task's
        actual rendered gold_sql
        at generation time; D.2's map only narrows which field+operation
        combinations are worth
        attempting to generate in the first place. Fault tests must exercise
        real constructed SQL strings
        through the scanner (e.g. a bare SELECT company FROM companies LIMIT 5 —
        field-agnostic,
        excluded regardless of which field's policy was consulted), not merely
        check whether a forbidden
        name string appears in a policy list.

     Taxonomy names (filter, aggregation, join, semantic_filter, plus the 3
     frozen held-out
     names): traced against every operation-shaped mention in README Phases 12,
     14, 18-26, 41 —
     aggregation and join are the document's own words for real mechanisms
     (README:264,539,541);
     no_match/abstention was checked and confirmed to be an evaluation-outcome
     axis (Phase 25),
     correctly excluded from this taxonomy. Independently cross-checked against
     v2's actual
     taxonomy.py (FILTER_LIST, AGGREGATE covering
     count/sum/group-by/argmax/top-k,
     SEMANTIC_FILTER for free-text columns) — the two sources converge on the
     same core names, and v2
     surfaces semantic_filter as the right category for
     companies.product_or_service (a free-text
     field with no v3 precedent otherwise). Still flagged for your explicit 
     sign-off since neither
     README nor v2 assembles this exact list as a single named per-field
     contract — Phase 9 is where it
     gets assembled for the first time, now grounded in two independent,
     converging sources rather than
     invented from nothing.

     D.3 Training eligibility. As above (layer 4), kept structurally separate
     from semantic validity
     (layer 1) so Phase 22's probe and future training generators consume the
     correct layer.

     D.4 SQL operation detection — comment-safe lexer, not raw stripping. A
     left-to-right scanner
     that replaces (never deletes) each '...' string literal, "..." / `...` /
     [...]
     quoted-identifier span, -- ... line comment, and /* ... */ block comment
     with a single space —
     preserving token boundaries so GROUP/**/BY becomes GROUP BY
     (space-separated), not GROUPBY
     (concatenated). Keyword-boundary regex (\bGROUP\s+BY\b, \bORDER\s+BY\b,
     \bLIMIT\b,
     case-insensitive) then runs on the cleaned remainder. Full test matrix:
     GROUP/**/BY (detect),
     GROUP\nBY (detect), GROUP  BY (detect), SELECT 'LIMIT' AS x (must NOT
     detect — inside string
     literal), SELECT "GROUP BY" FROM t (must NOT detect — quoted identifier),
     SELECT `GROUP BY` FROM t
     (must NOT detect — backtick identifier), SELECT [GROUP BY] FROM t (must NOT
     detect — bracket
     identifier), SELECT group_id FROM t (must NOT detect — word boundary
     already excludes this),
     escaped-quote cases ('it''s', "a""b") handled correctly by the scanner's
     escape-doubling rule.

     D.5 Exposure scanner. List-only: scan_strings(list[str]) -> report. A bare
     str raises
     TypeError naming the expected type — single, non-contradictory contract
     (Rev 1's self-contradiction
     is fully resolved, not just relabeled).

     D.6 Exposure-report assertions — three typed functions, not one generic 
     one. Each report shape
     already has its own evidence counter in the current code (strings_scanned,
     sql_scanned,
     sets_scanned/composition_violations — confirmed to exist now, not
     hypothetical):
     assert_value_scan_verified(report), assert_operation_scan_verified(report),
     assert_composition_scan_verified(report) — each hardcodes which fields must
     be present/consistent
     for its own shape. No caller ever names an arbitrary counter field, closing
     the
     counter="wrong_field" bypass. Four states per type: pending
     (scanned:false,count:null — valid,
     never a pass), verified-zero (scanned:true, evidence counter >0,
     exposure_count:0,
     internally consistent per-item/total), exposure-detected (fails), malformed
     (missing/inconsistent
     fields — fails). Scope-boundary test, added from the v2 lessons above:
     these scanners and
     assertions are exercised only against fine-tuning/training-time strings in
     tests; a fault test
     confirms the scanner is never invoked against the shared runtime value
     catalogue used by baselines
     like base_sql/base_sql_5shot at inference — that catalogue legitimately
     contains every value,
     held-out included, per the already-frozen exposure policy, and must never
     be misclassified as a
     violation the way v2's own writeup shows this distinction can be confused.

     D.7 Exposure normalization — NFKC, not NFC (verified, not assumed). Ran the
     actual case:
     unicodedata.normalize('NFC', 'ＡＳ９１００') returns the fullwidth string
     unchanged (does not
     equal 'AS9100'); NFKC on the same input correctly folds it to 'AS9100'. NFC
     only normalizes
     canonical equivalence (e.g. accented composition); it does not fold
     compatibility variants
     (fullwidth forms, and similar). Corrected pipeline:
     Unicode-compatibility-normalize (NFKC) →
     casefold → collapse internal whitespace runs → substring match, applied to
     every held-out literal
     against every model-visible rendered string (not only raw KB cells —
     rendering/copying can alter
     representation even from ASCII sources), confined to the scanning step only
     (never mutates the
     actual training text). "AS9100", "as9100", " AS9100 ", "ＡＳ９１００" all
     match; unrelated
     substrings do not. Flagged for approval since this is a real scientific
     definition of
     "exposure," not a mechanically-derived default — biased toward
     over-detection deliberately (a false
     positive costs one extra row to inspect; a false negative is an actual
     leak).

     D.8 Logical fingerprint (lfp2). Canonicalized logical_components folded
     into the hash.
     Commutative operands (two ANDed or two ORed predicates) sort before hashing
     so reordering doesn't
     change the fingerprint; the operator itself and any differing
     predicate/value do change it. Nested
     trees (A AND (B OR C) vs (A AND B) OR C) hash by canonical tree form, not
     flattened. Missing/
     incomplete logical_components fails closed rather than silently falling
     back to a weaker hash.

     D.9 Multipart representation — redesigned in this revision. The 
     UNION-ALL-with-discriminator
     design from Rev 3/4 is withdrawn; it doesn't work. Constructive proof:
     UNION ALL requires equal
     column arity across every branch, so a scalar part (val) and a two-column
     part (company, county)
     cannot share one result shape without padding; the shared part_id, val
     schema also throws away
     each part's real column names, forces every value through CAST(... AS TEXT)
     (turning 3 into
     "3", which the existing scalar grader's _SCALAR_OK type check would then
     treat as a different
     value than an untouched gold 3), and — worse — would require the model's 
     own predicted SQL to
     independently reproduce that exact discriminator/CAST convention just to be
     gradable, teaching an
     artificial SQL-shape requirement that has nothing to do with the actual
     question. Withdrawn.

     Replacement design: an ordered/keyed collection of independently-executed, 
     independently-typed
     per-part results — no shared schema, no discriminator, no casting.
     - gold_sql for a multi_part task is a dict keyed by part_id, one
       independently normal SQL
       string per declared part (e.g. {"count": "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM ...",
       "companies": "SELECT company FROM ..."}), each executed on its own,
       producing its own natural SQLResult
       with its own real column names and native types. This still honors Phase
       12's "D's target is a
       query" framing as its natural generalization for the multi-part case: a
       keyed sequence of
       queries, not one query straining to represent several shapes at once.
     - The model's predicted SQL for a multi-part task is a sequence of
       statements (split on
       top-level ; using the same comment/quote-aware lexer built for D.4, so a
       semicolon inside a
       string literal is never mistaken for a statement boundary), executed in
       the order the question
       presents the parts (order is part of the frozen task, known to both the
       model via the prompt and
       the grader via parts[] — nothing is invented at grading time). Each
       statement is paired
       positionally with the corresponding declared part.
     - Grading: a new thin wrapper, grade_multipart(item, pred_results: dict, 
       gold_results: dict) -> GradeResult, calls the existing, unmodified
       compare_results once per declared part (its own
       answer_type/target_columns), and requires every declared part correct —
       no new comparison
       algorithm, full reuse of frozen Phase 7 semantics per part.
     - Empty vs. omitted parts are now cleanly distinguishable, closing the Rev
       4 ambiguity: an emitted
       statement that executes and returns 0 rows is a legitimate empty-set
       answer for that part, graded
       normally; an omitted statement (fewer statements than declared parts) is
       a missing-required-part
       failure. No shared-table ambiguity to resolve.
     - Top-k ordering, real column names, and native types are preserved
       automatically — each part's
       SQLResult is exactly what that part's own SELECT naturally returns,
       nothing is regrouped or
       reinterpreted after the fact.
     - EvalRecord.execution_result for a multi-part item becomes a dict keyed by
       part_id, each value
       the natural (columns, rows) pair for that part — still one
       JSON-serializable field, still
       trivially round-trips through save/reload/regrade; the parts metadata
       field says which
       answer_type/target_columns apply to which key.
     - Modality-independent contract, addressing the layering concern directly:
       Phase 9 freezes the
       property that a multi-part answer is a part_id-keyed collection of 
       independently-typed
       part-results, each graded via the existing single-part compare_results 
       semantics using that
       part's own answer_type/target_columns. D produces this via a keyed
       sequence of independent
       SQL executions (above). How C's raw model completion gets parsed into 
       this same keyed-result
       shape remains a Phase 11/13 concern, correctly out of Phase 9's scope —
       but Phase 9 now freezes
       the target representation both modalities must produce, not just D's
       mechanism, so grading,
       EvalRecord, and regrading are written once and work for either modality
       without later
       reconciliation. (Confirmed: no v2 precedent exists for this either way —
       see Context.)

     D.10 Extra-part rule — settled now, not deferred. Extends the existing,
     already-frozen
     precedent (phase7_grader_tests.py's
     metrics_differ_semantic_right_schema_wrong: an extra column
     scores task_result_correctness=1.0 but strict_result_schema_accuracy=0.0):
     an extra,
     undeclared part present in the executed/tagged result beyond what parts[]
     declares does not
     fail task_result_correctness (each declared part is still graded
     independently and correctly) but
     does fail strict_result_schema_accuracy (output includes something outside
     the declared schema).
     Missing required parts[] metadata on a multi_part-typed item fails closed
     with a clear error —
     never silently falls back to legacy per-column grading. Legacy fallback
     (flattened
     target_columns-as-parts) applies only to items explicitly predating
     parts_list_v1 (a fixed,
     named allowlist of legacy fixture IDs, not "any item missing parts"), so a
     future generator bug
     that omits parts[] cannot silently masquerade as a legacy item.

     D.11 Grading. As D.9/D.10. GRADER_VERSION bumped grade_v3.0 → grade_v3.1.

     D.12 EvalRecord/result schema. Optional parts: tuple | None = None,
     backward-compatible
     from_dict default. build_fixtures() extended with a
     populated-execution_result multipart
     fixture pair specifically to prove regrade() recomputation: one
     deliberately-wrong multipart
     answer that the current (buggy) grader would have scored correct, regraded
     under the fixed
     grader to confirm it now scores incorrect — proving the regrade path
     genuinely recomputes rather
     than re-stamping provenance on a stale score.

     D.13 Verification/regrading. regrade() re-invokes
     compare_results/grade_structured
     against retained execution_result/gold (per-part where applicable) instead
     of keeping the
     recorded outcome for well-formed predictions. Raw prediction and gold
     remain untouched (existing
     _replace() invariant preserved).

     D.17 Multi-part execution-failure semantics — new in this revision, closing
     Gap #7/#8 from the
     Rev 5 coverage check. Amended once more after direct verification of three 
     follow-up corrections.
     Grounded in grade_v3.py's existing single-query contract (re-read in full):
     grade_structured
     re-raises X.ScopeError rather than swallowing it, checks whole-response
     degeneracy
     (classify_prediction_text, including stopped_at_max_new_tokens) before any
     parsing or
     execution happens at all, and otherwise reduces every failure to the
     existing closed status
     vocabulary via that same function. Multi-part grading reuses this exact
     machinery, adding only an
     aggregation rule across parts:
     - Whole-response truncation/degeneracy is checked once, before any 
       statement-splitting or
       execution — mirroring the single-query contract exactly (grade_v3.py's
       comment: "Partial or
       degenerate output is NEVER parsed or executed"). If
       classify_prediction_text returns a status for
       the raw multi-part response
       (truncated_output/generation_failure/invalid_output), the whole
       item takes that status immediately; the statement-splitter and every
       part's executor are never
       invoked. Regression test: a response flagged stopped_at_max_new_tokens
       must result in zero
       executor calls across all declared parts — verified by call-count, not
       just by final status.
     - Each declared part that survives the whole-response check is graded
       through the same,
       unmodified per-part pipeline (execute → compare_results) — no new
       failure-classification logic
       beyond the two additions below.
     - X.ScopeError is re-raised immediately if any part's execution raises it —
       never swallowed
       into a per-part failure status, preserving the existing invariant that a
       scope violation is a
       harness bug, not an ordinary incorrect answer.
     - An omitted required statement (D.9: fewer statements than declared parts)
       is classified as
       parse_failure for that part — consistent with the existing use of
       parse_failure for
       "prediction doesn't have the expected structure" (grade_structured's own
       "not a SELECT/WITH
       query" case), not a new category.
     - The full per-part failure set now explicitly includes timeout alongside
       SQL_error,
       parse_failure, generation_failure, invalid_output (the whole-response
       check already covers
       truncated_output) — timeout was missing from the Rev 6 list despite being
       one of CLAUDE.md's
       frozen eight statuses.
     - If every part executes and compares cleanly: overall status = "correct"
       iff every part is
       correct (already frozen in D.9/D.10), else "incorrect".
     - If one or more (post-whole-response-check) parts hit a per-part failure
       status: the whole item's
       task_result_correctness and strict_result_schema_accuracy are 0.0, and
       the top-level status
       is set from the first such failure by declared part order (a small,
       explicit, new tie-break —
       flagged for approval, analogous in spirit to the existing
       OPERATION_PRECEDENCE pattern already
       used elsewhere in holdout_v3.py) — never silently reclassified as plain
       "incorrect", since that
       would hide why it failed. Per-part failure details (which part, which
       status) are retained in
       error_detail, not discarded.
     - Fault/regression tests: whole-response truncation → zero executor calls
       (new); a correct first
       part followed by a SQL_error second part (must not score correct, must
       retain the real failure
       type); a timeout in a part (now covered, wasn't before); an omitted
       statement → parse_failure,
       not left unclassified; a ScopeError in any part (must propagate, not be
       caught); a parse_failure
       in a non-first part (tests the aggregation rule isn't just "check part
       0"); all-parts-correct
       baseline (must still score correct, no regression).

     D.18 Operation-heldout and compositional-heldout scanning must cover every 
     part, not the dict's
     keys — new in this revision, and this is a live, reproduced bug in the D.9 
     design, not a
     documentation gap. Reproduced directly: calling the existing
     scan_operations with a
     part_id-keyed gold_sql dict (as D.9 defines it) iterates the dict's keys
     ("count", "companies") as if they were SQL text — enumerate(strings) over a
     dict yields its
     keys. Verified with a synthetic two-part query where one part contains a
     bare LIMIT: passing the
     dict directly reports 0 exposures; passing list(gold_sql.values())
     correctly reports 1. This
     would have silently let a held-out construct into training the moment D.9
     shipped. Fix:
     - scan_operations/scan_compositions (and scan_strings, for symmetry with
       D.5) raise on a
       bare dict rather than silently iterating it — consistent with the
       list-only philosophy already
       adopted in D.5, fail loud instead of fail silent.
     - New dedicated wrapper, scan_operations_multipart(gold_sql: dict, reg),
       explicitly extracts
       gold_sql.values() before delegating to the existing (unmodified)
       scan_operations, then combines
       detected families across all parts using the existing frozen precedence
       (OPERATION_PRECEDENCE) — a multi-part task with group_by in one part and
       a clean filter in
       another is excluded from training entirely, exactly as a single-query
       task would be under the
       existing multi_family_rule. Per README:722, this check applies to D's SQL
       and C's metadata
       alike — C's metadata (once Phase 11/13 generates it) must be derived from
       the same complete,
       all-parts task evidence, not just part 1.
     - Constructs are never concatenated across parts before classification (an
       ORDER BY in one part
       and a LIMIT in a different part must not be misread as one argmax_topk
       query) — each part is
       classified independently, and the union of families found across parts is
       what's checked
       against the held-out set, not a merged/concatenated SQL string.
     - Fault tests: the exact reproduced case above (dict-direct call → must now
       raise, not silently
       return 0); a two-part task with a held-out construct in the non-first
       part → whole task excluded;
       a two-part task with clean SQL in both parts → not excluded; an ORDER BY
       in part A and LIMIT
       in part B (different parts) → must NOT be misclassified as a single
       argmax_topk construct.

     D.19 Compositional-heldout checking must use the whole task's component 
     union — new in this
     revision. Grounded directly in README's Phase 23 superset rule (re-read:
     "For each held-out set H
     and every training set T: assert not H ⊆ T") — a multi-part task is one
     logical training item, so
     its "training set T" for this purpose must be the union of every declared
     part's component usage,
     not each part checked in isolation. Confirmed by construction: a part
     carrying only
     {certifications} and a second part of the same task carrying only
     {processes} would each pass
     the held-out {certifications, processes} check individually while their
     union violates it — exactly
     the leak the superset rule exists to prevent. Fix: scan_compositions for a
     multi-part task is
     called once with the union of component sets declared across all of that
     task's parts, not once
     per part. Per-part structure and join-arity information are retained
     separately (for provenance and
     for D.9's independent-execution design) — the union is computed only for
     the composition check
     itself, and never used to invent a join that never actually occurred in any
     single part's SQL.
     Fault test: reproduced the exact case above — checking parts separately
     reports 0 violations;
     checking the task-level union reports 1 — confirming the union-based check
     is required, not optional.

     D.20 Gold/prediction identification contract for multipart D — made 
     explicit, not merely
     implied. D.9 already specifies gold as a part_id-keyed dict and the model's
     prediction as a
     positionally-ordered sequence of statements; this sub-contract freezes that
     pairing explicitly as
     its own named rule rather than leaving it as an incidental detail: parts[] 
     order is
     authoritative, and predicted statement N (1-indexed, in emission order) 
     belongs to declared part N.
     Test matrix, each case distinct from D.9's existing missing/extra-part
     tests: statements emitted out
     of the declared order (must be graded against the wrong part and therefore
     likely fail — this is a
     model-prediction quality issue, not a grading-contract bug, so the test
     confirms positional pairing
     is applied literally, not smartly reordered); too few statements
     (missing-part case, D.9); too many
     statements (extra-part case, D.10); a semicolon inside a quoted string
     literal (must not be
     misread as a statement boundary — reuses the D.4 lexer); an
     emitted-but-empty statement (a bare ;
     with nothing between two separators — treated as a parse_failure for that
     part, not a silently
     skipped one); duplicate or ambiguous part_ids in the task's own declared
     parts[] metadata (a
     task-authoring error — fails closed at task-validation time, before grading
     is even attempted).

     D.21 Insufficient-evidence regrading — new in this revision. The field 
     design is agreed (Codex has
     since clarified a ninth status was never a hard requirement, a separate 
     field is acceptable); what
     was still missing, and is verified as a real gap, is that the field alone 
     doesn't stop anything from
     consuming a historical score as if freshly verified. Confirmed the
     underlying constraint by
     re-reading regrade()'s own docstring: it deliberately does not re-execute
     SQL ("Phase 8 uses
     synthetic execution results rather than live inference"), so a record whose
     execution_result is
     None genuinely cannot have its score re-derived — there's nothing to
     recompute from. The core rule:
     never relabel a historical score as newly recomputed when the evidence 
     needed to recompute it is
     absent. Design: keep status within CLAUDE.md §25's frozen eight values,
     untouched, when
     evidence is insufficient — the original score stands as the historical
     record it always was. Add a
     separate, non-authoritative field, regrade_outcome, alongside
     status/grader_version/
     grader_sha256, with exactly two values regrade() can produce: "recomputed"
     or
     "insufficient_evidence". Dropped the earlier third value "not_attempted" —
     it was never actually
     defined (nothing in Rev 5/6 said when it would occur); a record simply
     defaults to regrade_outcome: None before regrade() ever touches it, so
     "never regraded" is the natural unset state, not a
     named enum member.

     Two further fixes, both verified against actual code rather than assumed:
     1. The gate must require the positive outcome, not merely reject the 
        negative one. My original
        assert_fully_regraded design only raised on regrade_outcome == 
        "insufficient_evidence" — a
        record with regrade_outcome still None (never regraded at all) would
        silently pass, which is
        exactly the same class of bug as the field-without-a-consumer gap this
        section already fixes once.
        Corrected: assert_fully_regraded(records, *, expected_grader_sha256)
        requires, for every
        record, r.regrade_outcome == "recomputed" and r.grader_sha256 == 
        expected_grader_sha256 —
        anything else (None, "insufficient_evidence", an unrecognized value, or
        a "recomputed" record
        whose grader_sha256 doesn't match the current expected grader) raises. A
        whitelist of the one
        acceptable state, not a blacklist of the one known-bad one.
     2. Historical grader provenance must be preserved, not just the score.
        Re-read regrade()'s
        actual current code: it unconditionally re-stamps
        grader_version/grader_sha256 to the new
        grader for every record via _replace(r, ..., 
        grader_version=G.GRADER_VERSION, grader_sha256=grader_sha256), even for
        the "well-formed prediction keeps its recorded outcome"
        path — meaning today's code would already mislabel an unverified
        historical score as if the
        current grader produced it. Fix: when a record's evidence is
        insufficient,
        grader_version/grader_sha256 (and status/the two scores) are left
        completely untouched —
        only regrade_outcome: "insufficient_evidence" is set. A record's
        provenance must never claim to
        originate from a grader that never actually evaluated it.

     Verified consumer gap, not hypothetical: I read eval_report_v3.py's
     summarize() directly — it
     computes scored/failed/task/schema purely from
     status/task_result_correctness/
     strict_result_schema_accuracy, with zero awareness of any regrade_outcome
     field. A record with a
     stale status="correct" and regrade_outcome="insufficient_evidence" would
     pass summarize()'s
     existing DenominatorError checks and be silently counted as an ordinary
     verified-correct item —
     exactly the "presented as freshly verified" failure mode. The field must be
     consumed, not just
     stored. Required additions:
     - eval_report_v3.summarize() gains an explicit regrade-coverage breakdown
       ({"recomputed": N, "insufficient_evidence": M, "not_yet_regraded": K},
       the third bucket counting
       None) computed alongside the existing denominator accounting — without 
       changing that
       accounting: an insufficient-evidence record still counts in scored/failed
       exactly per its
       retained status, is never dropped from the denominator, and is never
       treated as an automatic
       wrong answer.
     - eval_verify_v3.assert_fully_regraded(records, *, expected_grader_sha256)
       per fix 1 above — the
       strict whitelist gate. Any report-generation path that wants to label its
       output "freshly
       regraded"/"fully re-verified under the current grader" must call this
       first and fail loudly rather
       than certify a claim it can't back. A report that hasn't cleared this
       gate must instead present
       those records' scores explicitly labeled as historical/unverified, not
       folded silently into
       headline numbers.
     - finetune/eval_report_v3.py added to the file inventory (C) — not
       previously listed.
     - End-to-end test added: serialize → reload → regrade → verify → report, on
       a mixed batch
       including one insufficient-evidence record — confirms the record's
       original score/status/
       grader_version/grader_sha256 survive byte-identical, the coverage
       breakdown reports it
       distinctly, and assert_fully_regraded correctly raises for that batch.
       Additional regression
       cases per fix 1: a record with regrade_outcome: None → gate raises; a
       "recomputed" record whose
       grader_sha256 doesn't match the currently-expected grader → gate raises
       (stale recompute under an
       older grader build must not pass as fresh). Records needing no regrade at
       all (pre-execution failures like
       generation_failure/truncated_output, derivable from retained
       raw_output/stop-metadata alone)
       get regrade_outcome: "recomputed" since their classification never
       depended on
       execution_result. Flagged for your explicit sign-off, since the
       coverage-gate design (what
       exactly blocks a report from claiming "fully regraded") is a judgment
       call worth your confirmation,
       not a purely mechanical fix.

     H. Stop conditions

     - The optimizer diff (F) shows any unintended change to select_holdouts.
     - Full independent recomputation (F) produces a different 9-value set, or
       finds an eligible
       candidate that should have beaten a current winner.
     - The operation taxonomy (D.2), exposure normalization default (D.7), the
       multi-part
       simultaneous-failure precedence rule (D.17), or the regrade_outcome
       side-channel resolution to
       the closed-status-vocabulary conflict (D.21) are not approved as proposed
       — all four are
       explicitly flagged decisions, implementation pauses on these specific
       items pending confirmation.
     - Any currently-passing Phase 7, 8, or 9 gate/fault test regresses
       unexpectedly.
     - Any fix requires touching context_renderer_v3.py's scope-enforcement
       logic (exceeds scope).
     - Step 0's tag restoration produces a SHA other than
       b18313ae593995e8d415880603b3d355dd695ebd, or
       the exact-commit content differs from what was already diffed and
       confirmed identical above.

       824 +# Registry loading -- two APIs with genuinely different guara

       828 +#       unmodified selection pipeline above and compares it f
           +ield-for-field                                               
       829 +#       to the committed file, plus schema/upstream-hash chec

       830 +#       --check, fault tests and synthetic validation use.   
       831 +#                                                            
       832 +#   load_registry()  -- the production / Phase-10+ entry poin
           +t. Requires the                                              
       833 +#       candidate checks above to pass AND a separate, extern
           +ally-recorded                                                
       834 +#       approval anchor (PHASE9_APPROVAL.json) to exist and m
           +atch. Raises                                                 
       835 +#       Phase9NotApproved if the anchor is absent -- it never
           + returns a                                                   
       836 +#       partially-usable object with a pending flag. A file i
           +nside the same                                               
       837 +#       writable repo is not a cryptographic guarantee; this 
           +is a separately                                              
       838 +#       reviewed approval record anchored to the reviewed com
           +mit, not more.                                               
       839 +#                                                            
       840 +# Both return a VerifiedCandidateRegistry: deeply immutable (
           +stores canonical

           +er mutating a                                                
       842 +# returned section can never corrupt the stored original.    
       843 +# -----------------------------------------------------------

       844 +REQUIRED_REGISTRY_SECTIONS = (                               
       845 +    "registry", "phase", "policy_version", "frozen_date", "fr
           +ozen_inputs",

           +tion_holdouts",

       851 +                                                             
       852 +                                                             
       853 +class VerifiedCandidateRegistry:                             
       854 +    """Deeply-immutable registry handle. Stores only the cano
           +nical JSON text;                                             
       855 +    every read parses a fresh copy, so mutating a returned di
           +ct/list can never                                            
       856 +    corrupt what's stored here."""                           
       857 +                                                             
       858 +    __slots__ = ("_text",)                                   
       859 +                                                             
       860 +    def __init__(self, text: str):                           
       861 +        object.__setattr__(self, "_text", text)              
       862 +                                                             
       863 +    def __setattr__(self, name, value):                      
       864 +        raise AttributeError("VerifiedCandidateRegistry is im
           +mutable")                                                    
       865 +                                                             
       866 +    def _data(self) -> dict:                                 
       867 +        return json.loads(self._text)                        
       868 +                                                             
       869 +    def __getitem__(self, key):                              
       870 +        return self._data()[key]                             
       871 +                                                             
       872 +    def __contains__(self, key):                             
       873 +        return key in self._data()                           
       874 +                                                             
       875 +    def get(self, key, default=None):                        
       876 +        return self._data().get(key, default)                
       877 +                                                             
       878 +    def keys(self):                                          
       879 +        return self._data().keys()                           
       880 +                                                             
       881 +    def sha256(self) -> str:                                 
       882 +        return hashlib.sha256(self._text.encode("utf-8")).hex
           +digest()                                                     
       883 +                                                             
       884 +    def raw_text(self) -> str:                               
       885 +        return self._text                                    
       886 +                                                             
       887 +                                                             
       888 +def _verify_registry_schema(data: dict) -> None:             
       889 +    missing = [s for s in REQUIRED_REGISTRY_SECTIONS if s not
           + in data]                                                    
       890 +    if missing:                                              
       891 +        raise HoldoutError(f"registry missing required sectio
           +n(s): {missing}")                                            
       892 +    if data.get("policy_version") != POLICY_VERSION:         
       893 +        raise HoldoutError(                                  
       894 +            f"registry policy_version {data.get('policy_versi
           +on')!r} != "                                                 
       895 +            f"expected {POLICY_VERSION!r}")                  
       896 +    for f in MULTIVALUED:                                    
       897 +        sel = data.get("value_holdouts", {}).get(f, {}).get("
           +selected", [])                                               
       898 +        if len(sel) != len(set(sel)):                        
       899 +            raise HoldoutError(f"duplicate selected value(s) 
           +in {f}: {sel}")                                              
       900 +                                                             
       901 +                                                             
       902 +def _verify_upstream_inputs(data: dict) -> None:             
       903 +    frozen = data.get("frozen_inputs", {})                   
       904 +    for rel, expected in frozen.items():                     
       905 +        got = sha256_file(ROOT / rel)                        
       906 +        if got != expected:                                  
       907 +            raise HoldoutError(                              
       908 +                f"upstream input {rel} has drifted: registry 
           +expects "                                                    
       909 +                f"{expected}, current file hashes to {got}") 
       910 +                                                             
       911 +                                                             
       912 +def _load_and_verify_candidate(text: str) -> VerifiedCandidat
           +eRegistry:                                                   
       913 +    """Core verification against arbitrary registry text. Sep
           +arated from the                                              
       914 +    real-file loader below so fault tests can exercise reject
           +ion paths                                                    
       915 +    (stale/mutated/malformed registries) without touching the
           + real file."""                                               
       916 +    try:                                                     
       917 +        data = json.loads(text)                              
       918 +    except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError) as e:           
       919 +        raise HoldoutError(f"malformed registry JSON: {e}") f
           +rom e                                                        
       920 +    _verify_registry_schema(data)

          +r build.                                                      
      279 +

          +raded" / "fully

          +ing standing

      284 +    bad = []                                                  
      285 +    for r in records:

      296 +def regrade_coverage(records) -> dict:

          + list) else len(records),

  1. Missing extra-statement evidence still becomes a certified schema pass.

  true. But regrading defaults a missing flag to False; null also becomes       
  False.

  Retained evidence    Original schema score    Regraded schema score           
  Certified                                                                     
  Flag absent    0.0    1.0    Yes                                              
  Flag null    0.0    1.0    Yes                                                
  Flag true    0.0    0.0    Yes                                                
                                                                                
                                                                                
  Older records naturally lack this newly introduced field. Missing evidence    
  cannot mean “confirmed no extra statements.”

  reconstructed from other retained evidence. [Default-to-false branch (line

  recomputation.

  reproduced (same discipline as before — I ran the actual exploit before
  touching any code) and fixed:

  1. Missing/null extra_present defaulting to a certified pass — fixed by
     requiring an actual bool; anything else now forces insufficient_evidence
     and leaves the original score untouched.
  2. Multipart regrade skipping per-part metadata validation — confirmed via
     your exact full pipeline (serialize→reload→regrade→verify→report), the
     999-vs-1 case really did certify as "fully regraded." Fixed by applying the
     same validate_item_metadata check regrade uses for single-query items.
  3. Malformed scan inputs mixed with valid ones — scan_strings/scan_operations
     now reject any None entry outright rather than silently skipping it, and
     scan_compositions finally got the bare-string guard the other two scanners
     already had (confirmed it really was scanning 24 characters as 24 component
     sets).
  4. Fingerprint leaf accepting "field but no value" — the old check only
     counted keys; now it requires both field and value explicitly, stated
     plainly as my own implementation choice, not a claim about a frozen
     predicate schema.
  5. The stale-grader regression test not isolating what it claimed — you were
     right that it passed for the wrong reason (no retained evidence →
     insufficient_evidence regardless of grader identity). Fixed the fixture to
     carry real evidence, and while doing so found my own round-2 fixture (fx19)
     hit the exact "old record predating the field" scenario finding #1
     describes — fixed that too.

  Results: 52 Phase 9 gates + 99 fault checks (was 93) + --check (still
  verifying all 4 artifacts) + 81 Phase 7 checks (unchanged — grade_v3.py

❯ Re-audit of d17887e: the five reported examples are fixed, but Phase 9 is     
  still not ready for approval. Three broader validation/certification gaps     
  remain, plus one scan-evidence regression.                                    
  Confirmed progress                                                            
  I independently reran 52 Phase 9 gates, 99 fault checks, 81 Phase 7 checks,   
  and 86 Phase 8 checks. All pass.                                              
  The reported fixes behave correctly:                                          
  - Missing, null, or non-boolean extra_present preserves historical scores and 
  prevents certification.                                                       
  - The 999-versus-1 example now becomes invalid_output, with score zero.       
  - The reported malformed scan inputs and incomplete fingerprint leaf are      
  rejected.                                                                     
  - The stale-grader fixture now genuinely recomputes before testing identity   
  rejection.                                                                    
  Independent recomputation still confirms all nine holdouts are optimal.       
  Frozen inputs, selection functions, registry, ledger, and cost CSV are        
  unchanged. Documentation hash pins match.                                     
  Remaining blockers                                                            
  1. Certification does not identify the regrader implementation.               
  Round 3 changed eval_verify_v3.py, but certification checks only the hash of  
  grade_v3.py, which is unchanged.                                              
  I executed the actual Round 2 regrader in memory:                             
  Same retained evidence    Result                                              
  Round 2 recomputation    Incorrectly scored correct, 1.0                      
  Current certification gate inspecting that stored result    Accepted as       
  current                                                                       
  Actual Round 3 recomputation    invalid_output, 0.0                           
                                                                                
                                                                                
  Thus, old buggy recomputations can still be presented as current without      
  running the correction.                                                       
  Required fix: certification must identify the complete scoring/regrading      
  implementation—through a checked composite build identity, a separately       
  checked regrader identity, or an enforced fresh-recomputation path. Updating  
  Markdown hashes alone does not enforce this. [Certification gate (line        
  310)](/home/sm11926/GNEM_Finetuning/finetune/eval_verify_v3.py:310)           
  2. Regrading still accepts duplicate part IDs.                                
  Fresh grading rejects:                                                        
  parts = [                                                                     
      {"part_id": "p1", "answer_type": "scalar", "target_columns": ["n"]},      
      {"part_id": "p1", "answer_type": "scalar", "target_columns": ["n"]},      
  ]                                                                             
  But through JSON round-trip → regrade → verify → report, the same metadata    
  receives task 1.0, schema 1.0, certified. Regrading uses the same retained    
  result twice.                                                                 
  The added validator checks each part’s answer type and columns, but not the   
  complete multipart structure. Unique part IDs were explicitly included in the 
  previous requested correction.                                                
  Required fix: share complete multipart validation between fresh grading and   
  regrading, including part identity and uniqueness. [Regrade validation (line  
  217)](/home/sm11926/GNEM_Finetuning/finetune/eval_verify_v3.py:217)           
  3. Composition scanning still accepts malformed nested strings.               
  These still produce passing zero-violation certificates:                      
  scan_compositions(["certifications processes"], reg)                          
                                                                                
  scan_compositions_multipart(                                                  
      {"p1": "certifications", "p2": "processes"}, reg                          
  )                                                                             
  The outer-string guard works, but strings inside the collection are converted 
  into character sets.                                                          
  For comparison, correctly shaped input:                                       
  {"p1": ["certifications"], "p2": ["processes"]}                               
  correctly detects the held-out composition and fails.                         
  Required fix: validate each component collection before converting it to a    
  set, including values received by the multipart wrapper. Malformed shapes     
  must raise rather than certify zero violations. [Composition scanners (line   
  1162)](/home/sm11926/GNEM_Finetuning/finetune/holdout_v3.py:1162)             
  Additional regression                                                         
  scan_operations([""], reg) now reports one SQL item scanned and passes its    
  assertion. The previous commit reported zero evidence and rejected it.        
  An empty SQL string is not an executed query returning an empty result.       
  Reject blank SQL entries or exclude them from genuine evidence counts;        
  legitimate empty rendered prose is a separate case. [SQL evidence counter     
  (line 1134)](/home/sm11926/GNEM_Finetuning/finetune/holdout_v3.py:1134)       
  Decision                                                                      
  Keep Phase 9 unapproved. The remaining work is to complete shared validation  
  and make certification track the implementation that actually produced the    
  scores, with regression tests covering these cases.                           
  I changed no repository files. The worktree remains clean, the approval       
  anchor and Phase 10 remain absent, and the status remains Phase 9 / last      
  completed Phase 8.

● Verdict

  Confirmed and fixed — this one is worth naming plainly: round 6's own fix 
  introduced round 7's bug. Validating list(T) and then scanning the original T
  is safe for a list/tuple/set but silently empties an iterator or generator, so
  the validation pass I added last round was quietly breaking detection for any
  non-materialized input. Fixed by materializing each component collection to a
  list exactly once and using that same list for both validation and scanning.
  Added 16 regression tests (127 total now) covering the exact reported cases,
  generator equivalents, full list/tuple/set/iterator/generator equivalence for
  both held-out and held-in inputs, and malformed-member detection through a
  generator. Full suite green: 127 fault checks, 52 gates + --check, 81 Phase 7,
  91 Phase 8, independent recomputation still confirms all 9 values optimal.
  Committed as 6ac466d.

  This is now seven rounds (5 external + 2 self/audit-driven), and this round is
  qualitatively different from the first six: it's not a missed edge case in
  old code, it's a fresh bug introduced by the previous fix itself. That's a
  meaningfully worse signal about the correction process than "audit keeps
  finding narrower gaps" — it means each patch now carries its own risk of
  regression, not just incompleteness.

  Given that, my recommendation shifts from last time: I don't think another
  audit-fix-audit cycle on this same function is the efficient path anymore. Two
